interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you had to give a teammate difficult feedback.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A teammate had merged three PRs in one week without any tests on the changed logic, and one of them shipped a bug that took our on-call engineer about two hours to trace back to that change. I brought it to him directly, one on one, same week.

I structured it around the specific behavior, not his character: "the last three PRs didn't include tests for the logic you changed, and one of those caused a two-hour on-call investigation." I didn't say he'd been careless or sloppy — I named the observable pattern and its concrete cost. Then I was explicit about the ask: "going forward, I want every PR you open to include tests for whatever logic changed before requesting review."

He hadn't realized the pattern until I laid out all three together — he'd been treating each PR as a one-off exception under deadline pressure, not noticing it had become a habit. We agreed I'd flag it directly in review if it happened again rather than letting it build up to another conversation like this one.

It didn't come up again. What made the conversation land, I think, was leading with a specific, checkable behavior and its cost rather than a character judgment — that gave him something concrete to actually change, and nothing to get defensive about.

**Testing:** whether you can structure hard feedback around behavior and impact rather than character, and whether you actually followed through rather than just delivering a one-time complaint.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Feedback

interviewQuestions.question: Describe a time you had to de-escalate a heated disagreement in a meeting.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Two engineers were arguing about whether a new endpoint could hit its p99 latency target with a synchronous downstream call, and the conversation had gotten repetitive and a little sharp — both restating the same points louder rather than making new ones.

I stepped in without taking either side: "I think we're both making valid points and starting to talk past each other. Can we write down the actual disagreement? I believe it's whether we can hit p99 with a synchronous call, and you believe we can't. Can we timebox 20 minutes after this meeting to load-test it, and go with whichever the data supports?" Both agreed immediately — I think naming the disagreement plainly, rather than either of them having to restate their case again, gave everyone a face-saving way to stop arguing.

The load test showed the synchronous call missed the target under realistic load by about 40ms, so the async approach won — the person who'd been pushing sync accepted it without friction, since the resolution came from data rather than either of us being overruled by the other's persistence.

What I'd generalize from it: the move that actually cools a heated technical argument isn't arguing your position harder, it's converting a values disagreement into a checkable, factual one and proposing a concrete way to check it.

**Testing:** whether you have an actual de-escalation technique, versus just waiting out the argument or picking a side to end it faster.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: De-escalation

interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a conflict where you were right, but you'd handle the aftermath differently if you could do it again.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I was pushing for a service to move off a legacy job scheduler that had caused two outages that quarter. A teammate disagreed, mostly because he'd built the scheduler's retry logic himself and didn't want to see it retired. I had the stronger technical case and, over a couple of meetings, got the team to agree with me — we migrated, and it did meaningfully reduce incidents afterward.

Where I'd do it differently: I focused entirely on winning the technical argument and didn't spend any real effort on how he'd feel about his own work being replaced. After the migration, he pulled back from proposing infrastructure changes in general, and it took a few months before he was pushing new ideas as confidently as before — I don't think that was a coincidence.

If I were doing it again, I'd have looped him into designing the replacement rather than just building the case against his original design — giving him ownership over what came next, not just a technically superior counter-argument to what he'd already built. Being right about the architecture didn't require costing him that.

I've since made a habit, when I'm arguing to replace something a specific person built, of explicitly inviting them onto the redesign before I finalize the proposal — it costs me a little time and usually improves the design too.

**Testing:** whether you can honestly evaluate a conflict you "won" and identify a real relational cost, rather than defaulting to a clean-victory narrative.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Reflection

interviewQuestions.question: How would you handle it if two teams you work with both believed they should own a new piece of shared infrastructure?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat it as an under-specified interface problem before treating it as an ownership fight, because in my experience these disputes are rarely really about who gets credit — they're about each team not trusting that their specific requirements will be respected if the other team owns the thing.

Concretely, I'd propose one team own the caching layer as a service with a documented API contract, and get the other team's specific requirements — latency ceilings, eviction behavior, whatever mattered to their use case — written into that contract and reviewed by both leads before any code is built. That converts "who owns this" into "what does this need to guarantee," which is a calmer, more checkable disagreement than a turf dispute.

I've seen the alternative go badly: escalating straight to a director for an ownership ruling tends to leave the losing team feeling unheard rather than actually resolved, and it doesn't produce any of the specification work that prevents the same fight from recurring on the next shared system.

The part I'd want an interviewer to notice: the resolution isn't a compromise on who "wins" — it's recognizing that the conflict was standing in for a missing contract, and once the contract exists, the ownership question mostly stops mattering to either team.

**Testing:** whether you can resolve organizational-scale conflict through structure rather than authority, and whether you see the interpersonal friction as a symptom of something fixable underneath it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Org-scale conflict
